### Recommendation

**Recommended design: a listening-first app with three modes on one Listen screen, and three levels of customisation.**

1. **Home = one 120 pt Play/Continue button.** Under it, a three-part mode control: **Learn · Relax · Sleep**. A mini-player follows the learner across the tabs (Home, Library, My Words, Progress). This gives "very simple, one big Play button" without hiding any feature.
2. **Listen screen = karaoke.** The current sentence is about 32 pt (11") or 36 pt (13") at default Dynamic Type, at about 40% of the height. The current word has a soft background. There is a part timeline. The bottom bar has only Play, sentence back/forward, speed, sleep timer, 中文 and Explanations. In Learn mode, an answer bar of three equal **88 pt** buttons (I know · I don't know · Go on) sits above it. In landscape it splits into a "two thumbs" layout. Relax mode is the same screen with no answer bar and no mic: the teacher explains automatically and words become "learning".
3. **Explanation card = popover anchored to the word in regular width, medium-detent sheet in compact width.** This is exactly Apple's rule ("avoid popovers in compact views"). It closes by itself, as RULES.md requires, but every explanation is kept in a history panel and in My Words. "I know" always gets an Undo. A "hold to pause" countdown and an adjustable 3–15 s window answer Apple's warning about timed UI while keeping the learner's 5-second rule.
4. **Sleep mode = let the iPad lock.** It uses the Playback audio category, Now Playing on the Lock Screen, and a Live Activity timer with "+15 min". Timers: 10–90 min, end of part, end of chapter. There is a 60 s fade, one loudness level for all voices with −6 dB at night, and no sounds from the interface. If Play is pressed within 5 minutes of the timer ending, the timer starts again. In the morning, the app offers to continue from a little before you fell asleep (default 3 min, snapped to a sentence start). The proposed default is to explain nothing while asleep and save the words for a morning review; the learner must confirm this.
5. **Customisation = presets (Study / Relax / Sleep / my own), then about 8 simple settings on one page, then an "Advanced" page with search, then an "Edit buttons" mode.** In Edit buttons mode any button can be moved, resized (56/72/88 pt), relabelled, re-assigned or hidden, and the layout is saved to the account. Seven teaching characters sit on one picker. "My Teacher" (the learner's RULE ONE/TWO/THREE prompt) comes first and is the default. Every character has a 10-second sample and an editor with sliders, plus an advanced prompt editor.

**Why:**
- It follows Apple's current rules (iPadOS 27, HIG updated to Sep 2026) for popovers, sheets, 44 pt targets, Dynamic Type, Reduce Motion, background audio, and letting audio apps turn off the screen.
- It copies proven patterns:
  - Apple Books: mini-player, Line Guide, left/right menu position, Reset Theme.
  - Readwise Reader: in-context lookup panel, new UI kept optional.
  - Pocket Casts and BookPlayer: fade, end of chapter, +time, auto-restart, Live Activity.
  - Headspace: users miss parts while settling in.
- It keeps every rule in RULES.md.

**Build note:** make the sleep features native, or at least use real audio files plus Media Session in the web version. Home-screen web apps only got Screen Wake Lock in iPadOS 18.4, and (unverified) Safari speech voices are unreliable once the iPad locks.


### Fact-check of the key claims (an independent checker tried to disprove them)

- **confirmed**: Apple's HIG says to avoid popovers in compact views and use a sheet instead. A popover should point at the element that opened it, only one may show at a time, and work must be saved when a nonmodal popover closes automatically.
  - Evidence: I fetched the HIG JSON at https://developer.apple.com/tutorials/data/design/human-interface-guidelines/popovers.json, which backs https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/popovers. All four statements appear verbatim.
- **confirmed**: On iPadOS the HIG default control size is 44x44 pt (minimum 28x28). The default text size is 17 pt (minimum 11 pt). Minimum contrast is 4.5:1 for text up to 17 pt. The HIG also says to minimise time-boxed elements that auto-dismiss on a timer.
  - Evidence: I fetched https://developer.apple.com/tutorials/data/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility.json, which backs https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility. The figures above come from its tables and its Cognitive section.
- **confirmed**: Apple says most apps, including audio apps, should let the system turn off the screen. With the Playback audio category and the Audio background mode, audio continues when the device is locked.
  - Evidence: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/uikit/uiapplication/isidletimerdisabled (Important note). https://developer.apple.com/documentation/avfoundation/configuring-your-app-for-media-playback (sections on the audio session category and the background mode). I fetched both through their tutorials/data JSON endpoints.
- **confirmed**: The HIG tells apps to avoid repurposing audio controls (headphone and Lock Screen buttons). The remote commands available include play/pause, next/previous track, skip forward/back, change playback position, change rate and bookmark.
  - Evidence: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/playing-audio (fetched as JSON). https://developer.apple.com/documentation/mediaplayer/mpremotecommandcenter (fetched as JSON; bookmarkCommand is listed under 'Bookmarking a media item').
- **confirmed**: Pocket Casts iOS (open source, Oct 2026) fades out over 5 seconds when the sleep timer ends, has shake-to-restart and a +5 min button, and restarts the timer automatically if playback resumes within 5 minutes. BookPlayer offers 5/10/15/30/45/60 min and end of chapter.
  - Evidence: I read the source at https://github.com/Automattic/pocket-casts-ios/blob/trunk/podcasts/SleepTimerManager.swift, podcasts/SleepTimerViewController.swift, podcasts/PlaybackManager.swift (lines ~1786), podcasts/Settings.swift (lines 1015-1031) and podcasts/LiveActivity/ExtendSleepTimerLiveActivityIntent.swift. I also read https://github.com/TortugaPower/BookPlayer/blob/develop/BookPlayerWidgets/Phone/TimeListened/SleepTimerOption.swift and BookPlayer/Player/SleepTimer.swift.
- **confirmed**: iPadOS 27 is the current iPad OS. Apple Books on iPad offers a sleep timer, a configurable skip length, a swipe-down mini-player, a Line Guide that dims the rest of the page, a left/right Reading Menu Position, and Reset Theme.
  - Evidence: https://support.apple.com/guide/ipad/whats-new-in-ipados-27-ipad8d9d296d/ipados , https://support.apple.com/guide/ipad/listen-to-audiobooks-ipad9402fbe6/ipados and https://support.apple.com/guide/ipad/read-books-ipadc8494b6b/ipados all returned HTTP 200 (copyright 2026). WebFetch could not resolve support.apple.com, so I retrieved and read them with curl.
- **confirmed**: In Safari home-screen web apps, the Screen Wake Lock API works only from iOS/iPadOS 18.4. Before that it did not work in standalone home-screen apps. The Media Session API has been in Safari since version 15.
  - Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mdn/browser-compat-data/main/api/WakeLock.json and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mdn/browser-compat-data/main/api/MediaSession.json (current main branch, parsed directly).
- **corrected**: Readwise Reader (version 8.25, Oct 8 2026) added a Lookup panel. A long-press on a word or phrase explains it in a dedicated panel, and a term unique to the document is defined the way the author uses it. This is a direct precedent for Dream Book's in-context explanation card.
  - Correct / uncertain: The feature is described correctly, but the version is wrong. 'Lookup in Reader' first appears in the release notes of version 8.6 (Jun 5, 2026) and is repeated in later notes. Version 8.25 (Oct 8, 2026) is the current version, and there Lookup is listed only under 'Previously:'. What 8.25 actually adds is new TTS voices (beta), Reading Themes, GPT-6 Luna for Ghostreader summaries, YouTube chapters and faster loading of heavily highlighted books. The correct statement is: 'Readwise Reader added a Lookup panel in v8.6 (June 2026); it is still present in v8.25 (Oct 8, 2026).' The description is accurate: 'select (long press) any word or phrase and Reader explains it right away in a dedicated lookup panel... when you select a term (or name) unique to the document, get the definition the way the author uses it.' Calling it a precedent for Dream Book's explanation card is a fair design comparison, not a factual claim.
  - Evidence: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/readwise-reader/id1567599761 (retrieved with curl). The Version History lists 8.25 Oct 8 with Lookup under 'Previously:'. The 'Lookup in Reader' text appears in the notes for 8.6 (Jun 5), 8.7, 8.10, 8.11, 8.13, 8.14, 8.16, 8.18, 8.19, 8.20, 8.23 (Oct 1) and 8.25. It is absent from 8.5 (Jun 2). Note: the WebSearch budget for this turn was used up, so every check was made against primary sources fetched directly.


## R8. Account, cloud library and data that survive deleting the app


### Summary

Anything Dream Book saves only inside the iPad app is deleted with the app. To make everything come back after a reinstall, the app needs a copy online that is tied to an account, plus a few small things kept in Apple's iCloud Keychain. My recommendation: keep everything on the iPad first, so listening works offline, even in bed or on a plane. The app then copies every change quietly to Supabase in the background. Supabase is an online database with sign-in (Apple, Google or email), file storage for your books, and rules that let each person see only their own data. For you alone it can run on the free plan; for a public app it costs about $25 a month for 1,000 users and roughly $250 to $650 a month for 100,000 users. Your API key should go in iCloud Keychain, not online, and a paid subscription comes back by itself through the App Store. Apple's own iCloud database (CloudKit) is free and needs no sign-in, but your Intel Mac on macOS 13 cannot use Apple's modern sync engine for it, and it cannot give you the Google or email accounts you asked for. So CloudKit is a backup plan, mainly if Supabase turns out to be unreliable in mainland China. Firebase works too, but Google services are blocked in mainland China, and its costs have no hard limit. Before release, the app also needs in-app account deletion, a privacy policy, books kept strictly private to each user, and clear permission before any of your data is sent to an AI company.

## 1. What Dream Read stores today, and what is missing for sync

| Data | Mac file (`<userData>/data/`) | iPad web (IndexedDB `dream-read`) | Ready to sync? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Settings, incl. styles/characters (`ai.styles`), level model (`level.model`, a Beta model per frequency band) | `settings.json` | `kv` store | JSON shape is the same on both, but **no per-field timestamps** |
| Word statuses | `vocab.json` → `words: Record<lemma, 'known'\|'learning'\|'ignored'>`, `marked` ranges | `kv` | **No timestamps and no "deleted" markers (tombstones)**: deleting removes the key, so a sync cannot tell "deleted" from "never existed" |
| My Vocabulary | `vocabulary.json` → `entries[lemma]: VocabEntry` (sentence, explanation, chinese, bookId, position, createdAt, lastSeenAt, timesExplained, status, level, again) | `kv` | Good: `mergeEntry()` already defines a merge (keep the first sentence, the latest explanation wins, add up the counts, known stays known) |
| Library + positions | `library.json` → `LibraryItem` (id, title, kind, addedAt, lastOpenedAt, position `{chapter,paragraph,sentence}`, percent) | `kv` | Book id = first 24 hex characters of SHA-256 of the file, the same on both platforms |
| Processed books | `books/<id>.json.gz` | `books` store | Large. Positions only match if both apps use the same importer and segmenter |
| AI chapter hints | `hints/<bookId>` | `hints` store | Cache: it costs money to rebuild, so it is worth syncing |
| AI usage | `usage.json` (last 5,000 records) | `kv` | Records have no ids |
| API keys | `secrets.json` + `secret.key` (AES-256-GCM) | **plain text** in IndexedDB | Must **not** be synced in plain text |
| CSV | `~/Documents/Dream Read/my-vocabulary.csv`: `word, chinese, explanation, sentence, book, chapter, date, status` | Export through the share sheet | **Loses data**: it has the surface word, not the lemma; the date only (YYYY-MM-DD); no bookId, position or counts |

To make the data syncable, the record shapes need: an `updatedAt` (and a "set by the learner on purpose" flag) for each word status, tombstones (`deleted: true` plus a time), ids for usage records, and a sentence "fingerprint" (a short hash of the sentence text) saved next to each position, so a position can be found again if the importer changes.

## 2. What survives deleting the iPad app?

| Where data lives | Deleted with the app? | Back after reinstall / on a new iPad? | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| App sandbox (SQLite, UserDefaults, files, WKWebView IndexedDB) | **Yes** | No (only if the whole iPad is restored from a backup) | The normal local store |
| iPad home-screen web app (today's PWA) storage | Most likely yes, when the icon is removed **(from memory, unverified)** | No | Today's iPad version keeps everything here |
| Keychain item (not synced) | No: on iOS, Keychain items have long stayed after an app is deleted **(from memory, unverified; Apple does not promise it)** | Same iPad only | Use it as a convenience, never as the only backup |
| **iCloud Keychain** (`kSecAttrSynchronizable = true`) | No | **Yes, also on other devices**, when iCloud Keychain is on | Since iOS 14 it syncs passwords, certificates and keys. It cannot be combined with `…ThisDeviceOnly` accessibility. Updating or deleting it changes every copy **(verified)** [Apple](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/security/ksecattrsynchronizable) |
| `NSUbiquitousKeyValueStore` (iCloud key-value store) | No | Yes (same Apple Account) | **1,024 keys, 1 MB in total, stored unencrypted on disk; Apple says not to put personal or sensitive data in it** **(verified)** [Apple](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/foundation/nsubiquitouskeyvaluestore). Good for a small marker like "this person had an account: Apple sign-in" |
| CloudKit private database | No | Yes | Counts against **the user's** iCloud storage; **not visible to the developer** **(verified)** [Apple](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/cloudkit/ckdatabase/scope/private) |
| iCloud Drive app folder | No | Yes | The user can see and delete these files in the Files app |
| Supabase / Firebase | No | Yes, after signing in | Needs an account |
| StoreKit purchases and subscriptions | No | Yes (`Transaction.currentEntitlements`, a "Restore Purchases" button) | Tied to the Apple Account, no own account needed |

## 3. Option A: Apple only (CloudKit, iCloud key-value store, iCloud Drive, iCloud Keychain)

- **Cost:** Apple says private data is stored "in your users' iCloud accounts for limitless scale"; public data gets up to 1 PB [Apple CloudKit](https://developer.apple.com/icloud/cloudkit/). The developer pays nothing for the private database; you only need the Apple Developer Program ($99 a year, from memory). Users get **5 GB of iCloud free**. iCloud+ costs $0.99, $2.99, $9.99, $29.99 or $59.99 a month in the US (50 GB, 200 GB, 2 TB, 6 TB, 12 TB), and ¥6, ¥21, ¥68, ¥198 or ¥398 in mainland China **(verified)** [Apple](https://support.apple.com/en-us/108047). Many people's free 5 GB is already full of photos, so sync can fail ("quota exceeded"), and the app must handle that calmly.
- **Engines:** `CKSyncEngine` handles pushing and pulling. It needs **iOS/iPadOS 17+ and macOS 14+**, sends at most **250 records per request**, and its schedule depends on system conditions, so call `fetchChanges` or `sendChanges` when you need a sync right now **(verified)** [Apple](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/cloudkit/cksyncengine-5sie5). SwiftData with CloudKit is simpler, but it **cannot enforce unique fields**, every relationship must be optional, and the schema can only grow (no deleting or changing fields after release) **(verified)** [Apple](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftdata/syncing-model-data-across-a-persons-devices). Book files fit as `CKAsset`s. Fetched assets sit in a temporary staging folder, so copy them out at once **(verified)** [Apple](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/cloudkit/ckasset).
- **Pros:** free; no sign-in screen (the Apple Account is already there), which fits "calm, everything automatic"; the developer cannot read users' data, which is good for privacy; **works in mainland China**, where iCloud is operated by GCBD (AIPO Cloud (Guizhou) Technology Co. Ltd.) **(verified)** [Apple](https://support.apple.com/en-us/111754).
- **Cons for this learner:** (1) **The Intel MacBook Pro on macOS 13 Ventura cannot run CKSyncEngine (macOS 14+)**, and the Electron Dream Read app could only use CloudKit JS (the web version, with an Apple ID sign-in) [Apple CloudKit JS](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/cloudkitjs), which is awkward. iPad apps run on Macs only with Apple Silicon. (2) RULES.md §9 asks for "an account (Google, Apple or email)"; CloudKit is Apple-only, so no Android, Windows or plain web later. (3) Users who are not signed in to iCloud, or whose storage is full, get no backup. (4) No server-side merge logic and no admin view for support.

## 4. Option B: Supabase (Postgres, Auth, Storage)

- **Prices (verified, [supabase.com/pricing](https://supabase.com/pricing)):**
  - **Free $0:** 50,000 monthly active users (MAU), 500 MB database, 1 GB file storage, 5 GB egress (download traffic), 50 MB maximum upload size, and "**paused after 1 week of inactivity**", with at most 2 active projects.
  - **Pro from $25 a month:** 100,000 MAU, then $0.00325 per MAU; 8 GB disk, then $0.125 per GB; 250 GB egress, then $0.09 per GB; 250 GB cached egress, then $0.03 per GB; 100 GB file storage, then $0.0213 per GB; daily backups kept 7 days; $10 a month of compute credit, which covers one Micro instance (1 GB RAM).
  - **Compute sizes:** Small $15, Medium $60, Large $110, XL $210 a month. Team plan $599 a month.
  - The Pro plan has a **spend cap that is on by default** **(verified)** [Supabase billing](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/platform/billing-on-supabase).
- **Auth:** Sign in with Apple (native on iOS with `signInWithIdToken`; the web/OAuth flow, which the Electron Mac app would use, **needs a new Apple secret key every 6 months**; the native-only flow does not) **(verified)** [Supabase Apple docs](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/social-login/auth-apple). Google and email sign-in and anonymous sign-ins are on the Free plan **(verified, pricing page)**.
- **Row-level security (RLS)** makes each user see only their own rows:

  ```sql
  alter table word_status enable row level security;
  create policy own on word_status for all
    using (user_id = (select auth.uid())) with check (user_id = (select auth.uid()));
  ```

  Storage works the same way: a private `books` bucket with paths `{user_id}/{book_id}.epub`, and a policy that the first folder of the path must equal `auth.uid()::text`.
- **Account deletion:** "You cannot delete a user if they are the owner of any objects in Supabase Storage", so delete the files first, then call `auth.admin.deleteUser()` from a server function **(verified)** [Supabase](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/managing-user-data).
- **Regions** include Singapore, Tokyo, Seoul, Mumbai, Sydney, Frankfurt, Ireland, Virginia and others **(verified)** [Supabase regions](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/platform/regions).
- **SDKs:** `@supabase/supabase-js` 2.118.0 (published 2026-10-15, npm) works in the Electron main process (Node 24) and in a Capacitor web view. supabase-swift exists for a native app (version not checked).
- **Mainland China:** reachability of `*.supabase.co` from mainland China is **uncertain** (there are reports of intermittent blocking, from memory). Test it from the learner's network before committing.

## 5. Option C: Firebase (Auth, Firestore, Cloud Storage)

- Auth is free up to 50K MAU; phone sign-in is billed per SMS **(verified)** [firebase.google.com/pricing](https://firebase.google.com/pricing).
- **Firestore free tier:** 1 GiB stored, 50,000 reads, 20,000 writes and 20,000 deletes per day, and 10 GiB of outbound transfer per month. After that, in us-central1: **reads $0.03, writes $0.09 and deletes $0.01 per 100,000**, and storage ≈ $0.15 per GiB-month (shown as $0.000205479 per GiB-hour) **(verified)** [Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/firestore/pricing). Internet egress is $0.12 per GiB from 10 GiB to 1 TiB ($0.23 to China destinations).
- **Cloud Storage for Firebase is "Not applicable" on the free Spark plan, so it needs Blaze (pay as you go).** Free amounts are 5 GB-months and 100 GB of downloads a month, only in us-central1, us-west1 and us-east1 **(verified)**. Standard storage is about $0.02 per GiB-month [Google Cloud Storage](https://cloud.google.com/storage/pricing).
- **Risk:** budgets only send alerts: "Requests to Firestore … will succeed even if you have exceeded your monthly … budget" **(verified)**. Billing per document punishes careless listeners. For example, re-reading 20,000 word documents on every launch costs about $0.006 per launch per user, which adds up fast at scale.
- **Google and Firebase services are blocked in mainland China** (widely known, not re-checked). That alone makes Firebase a poor fit given the learner's China ties. The JS SDK `firebase` is at 13.0.0 (2026-10-07).

## 6. Option D: hybrid, local-first SQLite with background sync (the recommended shape)

- **The local database is the truth.** The screens read and write local SQLite only. Sleep listening, airplane mode and bad networks never block anything. Each change also goes into an `outbox` table.
- **Push:** send outbox batches of up to 500 to one server function, `sync_push(ops jsonb)`, which applies the merge rules (section 7) in one transaction.
- **Pull:** `sync_pull(since_rev)` returns the rows whose server revision is higher than the last one this device has seen. A server sequence or trigger sets that revision, so a wrong device clock can never skip changes.
- **When to sync:** on app open, 3 seconds after a change, after each explanation, at the end of each chapter, while background audio is playing (the app is awake then anyway), and when the app goes to the background.
- **Local store:** for a native Swift app, GRDB/SQLite (or SwiftData if you go Apple-only). For a Capacitor app reusing `src/core`, use `@capacitor-community/sqlite` 8.1.1 (2026-08-06) with `@capacitor/core` 8.5.3 (2026-10-07). Do **not** rely on WKWebView IndexedDB as the only store.
- **Off-the-shelf engine:** PowerSync (local SQLite synced with Postgres, SDKs for Swift and Capacitor: `@powersync/capacitor` 0.9.4 and `@powersync/web` 2.5.0, both 2026-10-19). Free: 2 GB synced a month, 50 peak connected clients, deactivated after 1 week without activity. **Pro from $49 a month:** 30 GB synced, 1,000 peak clients, then $1 per GB and $30 per 1,000 clients **(verified)** [powersync.com/pricing](https://www.powersync.com/pricing). It is worth it only if the hand-made sync gives trouble, because each user's data is small (a few MB).

### Comparison

| | CloudKit | Supabase | Firebase | Supabase + PowerSync |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Survives app deletion | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Login needed | No (Apple Account) | Yes (Apple / Google / email; anonymous possible) | Yes | Yes |
| Works with the Electron Mac app on Intel / macOS 13 | Poorly (CloudKit JS only) | **Yes** (supabase-js) | Yes | Yes |
| Mainland China | **Works** (GCBD) | Uncertain | Blocked | Uncertain |
| Merge rules enforced on the server | No | **Yes** (SQL functions) | Partly (transactions and rules) | Yes |
| Cost limit | Free | Spend cap by default | Alerts only | Two bills |
| Android / web later | No | Yes | Yes | Yes |

## 7. Conflict handling (word known/learning across devices)

| Data | Rule |
|---|---|
| **Word status** | Each change carries `(time, explicit?)`. Explicit actions ("I know", double tap, the Vocabulary or Progress page) win by the **latest time**. An automatic "learning" (set when a word was explained) **never overrides "known"**, the same rule as today's `upsertEntry`, "learning unless the learner already knows the word". Examples: iPad offline sets *known* at 23:00 and the Mac auto-sets *learning* at 23:10 → known stays. The Mac sets *learning* on purpose at 23:30 → learning wins. |
| **My Vocabulary** | Keep an append-only table of **explanation events**. Merging is a simple union: the first sentence comes from the earliest event, the explanation and Chinese from the newest, `timesExplained` is the number of events, `again` is the number of "I don't know" events. This gives exactly `mergeEntry()`'s result, without lost counts. |
| **Reading position** | The latest change wins. Also keep each device's furthest point and show "You got further on the Mac (Chapter 7). Go there?" (Kindle-style). |
| **Settings** | Last write wins **per field** (flattened paths such as `voice.rate`, `listen.commandWindowMs`), which matches the `deepMerge` patches. |
| **7 teaching characters** | Last write wins per character and per field, plus the **last 20 versions of each prompt** kept for "Restore", because the prompts are hand-written. Deleted characters are tombstones. |
| **Level** | Sync the raw "I know / I don't know" answers (with frequency band and time) and recompute the Beta model on each device. Never let the whole model overwrite another device's (it would lose one device's evidence; `adapt.ts` also decays evidence weekly). |
| **Library** | Union. Delete = tombstone with a time. Adding the same file again (same SHA-256 id) removes the tombstone. |
| **AI caches** (hints, whole-book analysis) | Fixed per (book id, model, prompt version). The first upload wins and they never conflict. They save real AI cost after a reinstall. |
| **Usage records, marked ranges** | Append-only with UUIDs; union. |

### Suggested tables (all with `user_id`, RLS, `updated_at`, `rev`, `deleted`)

- `profiles` (level, native language)
- `settings_kv` (`key`, `value jsonb`)
- `characters` and `character_versions`
- `books` (`id` = sha24, title, kind, words, `file_path`, `encrypted`)
- `positions` (`book_id`, chapter, paragraph, sentence, `sentence_fp`, percent, `device_id`)
- `word_status` (`lemma`, status, `explicit`)
- `vocab_events`
- `level_answers`
- `ai_cache` (`book_id`, `kind`, `version`, storage path)
- `usage`

## 8. API keys and subscription

- **Personal use (bring your own key):** store the key as an **iCloud Keychain item** (`kSecAttrSynchronizable = true`, `kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlock`). It comes back after a reinstall and on new devices when iCloud Keychain is on. Never put raw keys in Supabase. Keychain access is tied to the developer Team ID, so pick the developer account (individual or organisation) before launch.
- **Public app:** a StoreKit 2 subscription. Entitlements come back by themselves after a reinstall, and you add a "Restore Purchases" button. Link it to the Supabase user with `appAccountToken` = user UUID. AI calls then go through a server function that holds the developer's key, never a key shipped inside the app.
- Anthropic does not serve mainland China, so neither a personal Claude key nor a Claude-backed subscription can legitimately serve users there.

## 9. Privacy and legal basics

- **App Store rules (guidelines last updated 16 Oct 2026, verified)** [Apple](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/):
  - 5.1.1(v): "If your app supports account creation, you must also offer account deletion within the app."
  - 4.8: if Google login is used, you must also offer an equivalent login that collects only name and email, lets the user hide their email, and does no ad tracking (Sign in with Apple qualifies).
  - 5.1.2(i): you must "clearly disclose where personal data will be shared with third parties, **including with third-party AI**, and obtain explicit permission."
- **Account deletion page (verified)** [Apple](https://developer.apple.com/support/offering-account-deletion-in-your-app/): deletion must be easy to find and must delete the whole account (deactivating is not enough). Apps with Sign in with Apple should **revoke the user's tokens through the REST API**. Explain that a subscription keeps billing through Apple until the user cancels it.
- **Copyright of uploaded books:** private per-user storage only, so no sharing, no public links (signed links that expire quickly), and no merging of identical files across users; terms saying users must own the rights; a takedown contact. In the US, registering a DMCA agent costs $6 and is renewed every 3 years (from memory). Import DRM-free EPUB and PDF only; never remove DRM. Optional: encrypt book files on the device (AES-GCM, key in iCloud Keychain), so the server holds unreadable bytes. If the key is lost, the user re-adds the file, and the same id brings back all the progress. Lowest-exposure alternative: keep book files in the user's own iCloud Drive app folder, and only vocabulary and progress in Supabase.
- **GDPR (EU users):** legal basis = providing the service (contract); privacy policy; data processing agreement (DPA) with the provider; EU region if needed; access and export (the JSON and CSV export already exist); erasure through account deletion; encryption in transit and at rest.
- **China PIPL (from memory, unverified):** separate consent before sending personal data abroad. The March 2024 CAC rules exempt a non-critical operator sending non-sensitive data of fewer than 100,000 people a year from the security assessment and the standard contract. Account deletion must be easy. Publishing in the China App Store needs an ICP filing, and generative-AI apps need extra approval, so **leave the China storefront out at first**.

## 10. Costs (monthly, estimated)

Assumptions:
- **"Engaged" user:** 10 MB of rows, 40 MB of book files, 3,000 writes and 5,000 reads a month, 10 MB egress.
- **"Mixed" average at 100k users:** 3 MB of rows, 10 MB of books, 40% active each month, 1 TB egress in total.

| Users | CloudKit | Supabase | Firebase (Blaze, us-central1) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1 (the learner)** | $0 | $0 (Free; pauses after 7 idle days) | $0 to $1 (Storage needs Blaze) |
| **1,000 engaged** | $0 to the developer | **≈ $25** (Pro $25 + 2 GB extra disk × $0.125 = $0.25; storage and egress within the allowance) | **≈ $5** (storage 9 GiB × $0.15 = $1.35; 2.4M writes = $2.16; 3.5M reads = $1.05; 35 GB files ≈ $0.70). It can be 10 to 100 times more if listeners are careless |
| **100,000 mixed** | $0 | **≈ $250** ($25 + Large compute $110 − $10 credit + 292 GB disk $36.50 + 900 GB files $19 + 750 GB egress $67.50) | **≈ $350** (120M writes $108 + 200M reads $60 + 300 GiB $45 + 1 TB files $20 + ≈ $120 egress) |
| **100,000 engaged (heavy)** | $0 | **≈ $650** (XL compute, 1 TB disk $124, 4 TB files $83, 2 TB egress $158, 120k MAU = $65 over) | **≈ $900** |

Adding PowerSync to Supabase: $49+ a month, plus about $1 per GB synced above 30 GB. **AI calls will cost far more than storage** in every scenario, so cache the AI results (whole-book analysis, hints) in the cloud.

## 11. Syncing with the Mac app (Dream Read)

1. **Now, no server:** a "Backup" button on the Mac writes one `dream-read-backup.json` (`settings`, `vocab`, `vocabulary`, `library` positions, `hints`, optionally `books/*.json.gz`) to iCloud Drive. Dream Book imports it with the Files picker (the route in `IPAD.md` §5). Use `vocabulary.json`, not the CSV; the CSV is a lossy last resort (the lemma must be rebuilt from the dictionary).
2. **With Supabase:** add a sync module to the Electron main process (supabase-js; keep the session in the existing AES `secrets.ts` store) that maps the JsonStore files to the same tables. JSON changes that do not break old files:
   - add `wordsMeta: Record<lemma,{t, explicit}>` next to `VocabState.words`;
   - use tombstones instead of deleting keys;
   - add UUIDs to usage records;
   - add `importerVersion` and `sentence_fp` to positions.
3. **Positions:** `{chapter, paragraph, sentence}` only match when both apps use the same TypeScript importers and segmenter. Either reuse `src/core` in Dream Book, or sync the processed `books/<id>.json.gz` as the canonical text (this keeps positions identical across platforms), and keep the fingerprint to find a sentence again after changes.
4. **Mac sign-in:** use Google or an email code (Apple OAuth on the web needs the 6-month secret renewal), and link identities to the iPad's Apple sign-in through Supabase identity linking.

## 12. Main uncertainties

- Whether `supabase.co` is reachable from mainland China: test it first.
- Keychain items surviving app deletion: long-standing behaviour, but not promised by Apple.
- Exact deletion behaviour of home-screen web-app storage.
- PIPL thresholds and China App Store rules (from memory).
- The supabase-swift version (not checked).
- Compute sizes at 100k users are rough guesses.

### Recommendation

**Build it in this order:** first the data on the iPad, then a copy online with Supabase, then small extras from Apple. CloudKit stays ready as a second option behind the same code.

1. **On the iPad (from day one):** SQLite is the only place the screens read and write, so hands-free sleep listening never waits for the network. Every row has `updated_at`, `deleted` (a tombstone, so deletions also sync) and `device_id`. Every change also goes into an outbox table, a list of changes still to upload.
2. **Online:** use Supabase.
   - Sign-in: native Sign in with Apple as the main one-tap button; Google and an email code as the other choices, as RULES.md §9 asks.
   - Data: a Postgres database with row-level security on every table, so each user sees only their own rows.
   - Books: a private Storage bucket with one folder per user.
   - Sync: two server functions, `sync_push` and `sync_pull`. `sync_push` applies the merge rules from section 7: "known" is never overwritten by an automatic "learning"; vocabulary is a list of events that only grows; settings keep the newest change per field; the level is recomputed from the learner's answers.
   - Region: Singapore or Tokyo if most users are in Asia; Frankfurt for the EU.
   - Plan: the Free plan while it is just you. Pro ($25 a month, spend cap on) before any public release, because the Free plan pauses after 7 idle days and has no backups.
3. **Small things from Apple:**
   - Put API keys in iCloud Keychain as a synced item (`kSecAttrSynchronizable`), never on the server.
   - Store a tiny marker in the iCloud key-value store, such as `hasAccount: apple`. After a reinstall the app opens with "Welcome back. Continue with Apple": one tap, Face ID, then vocabulary and progress download in seconds and books download when opened.
   - For a public app, use a StoreKit 2 subscription, which comes back by itself after a reinstall.
4. **Mac app (Dream Read):** first a backup JSON file through iCloud Drive (vocabulary.json, not the CSV). Then a sync module in the Electron main process using the same Supabase tables, with backward-compatible JSON additions: `wordsMeta` timestamps, tombstones, usage ids, sentence fingerprints.
5. **Before release:**
   - In-app account deletion: delete the storage files, then the rows, then the user, then revoke the Sign in with Apple tokens.
   - A privacy policy and the App Store privacy labels.
   - Explicit permission before any data goes to Claude or OpenAI (rule 5.1.2(i)).
   - Books stay private to each user, DRM-free files only, with an optional encryption switch on the device.
   - Leave out the China App Store at first.

**Why not the others:**
- **CloudKit** is free and works in China, but your Intel Mac on macOS 13 cannot use its sync engine (it needs macOS 14), and it cannot give Google or email accounts. Keep the sync code behind one interface (`SyncBackend`) so CloudKit can be swapped in if Supabase is unreliable from mainland China. **Test Supabase from your own network first.**
- **Firebase** is blocked in mainland China, charges per document read, and its budgets only send alerts; nothing stops the spending.

**Test before shipping:** add a book, mark words, delete the app, reinstall, sign in, and check that everything came back. Then make changes on two devices while both are offline and reconnect them. Then delete the account.


### Fact-check of the key claims (an independent checker tried to disprove them)

- **confirmed**: Supabase Free: $0, 50,000 MAU, 500 MB database, 1 GB file storage, 5 GB egress, 50 MB maximum upload, and free projects are paused after 1 week of inactivity. Pro: from $25 a month, 100,000 MAU then $0.00325/MAU, 8 GB disk then $0.125/GB, 100 GB file storage then $0.0213/GB, 250 GB egress then $0.09/GB, with $10 a month of compute credit. The Pro spend cap is on by default.
  - Evidence: Fetched https://supabase.com/pricing (2026-10-20). It says: 'Free $0/month ... 50,000 monthly active users, 500 MB database size ... 5 GB egress, 5 GB cached egress, 1 GB file storage ... Free projects are paused after 1 week of inactivity. Limit of 2 active projects'; 'Max file upload size 50 MB' (Free); 'Pro From $25/month ... 100,000 MAU then $0.00325 per MAU; 8 GB disk size per project then $0.125 per GB; 250 GB egress then $0.09 per GB; 100 GB file storage then $0.0213 per GB'; 'Paid plans include $10/mo in compute credits'; 'The Pro Plan has a spend cap enabled by default'. https://supabase.com/docs/guides/platform/billing-on-supabase repeats the same quotas.
- **confirmed**: CloudKit private-database records are owner-only, not visible to the developer, and counted against the owner's iCloud storage quota. iCloud gives 5 GB free; iCloud+ 50 GB costs $0.99/month in the US and ¥6 in mainland China.
  - Evidence: Apple doc JSON for https://developer.apple.com/documentation/cloudkit/ckdatabase/scope/private: 'Records in a private database: By default are owner readable and owner writable. Are not visible to the application developer via the Developer Portal. Are counted towards the owner's iCloud account storage quota.' https://support.apple.com/en-us/108047 (published Sept 16, 2026): 'with 5 GB of storage for free'; 'United States (USD) $0.99 [50 GB] $2.99 $9.99 $29.99 $59.99'; 'China mainland (CNY) ¥6 ¥21 ¥68 ¥198 ¥398'.
- **confirmed**: CKSyncEngine requires iOS/iPadOS 17+ and macOS 14+, and allows at most 250 records per request, so it cannot run on the learner's Intel Mac on macOS 13 Ventura.
  - Evidence: Apple doc JSON for https://developer.apple.com/documentation/cloudkit/cksyncengine-5sie5 lists platforms iOS 17.0, iPadOS 17.0, Mac Catalyst 17.0, macOS 14.0, tvOS 17.0, watchOS 10.0. The text says: 'Each batch is bounded by the server's per-request limit of 250 records (saves plus deletes combined); a batch that exceeds the limit fails with limitExceeded.'
- **confirmed**: NSUbiquitousKeyValueStore is limited to 1,024 keys and 1 MB in total, stores values unencrypted, and Apple says to keep sensitive data in the Keychain instead. Synchronizable Keychain items (kSecAttrSynchronizable) sync through iCloud Keychain and cannot use ThisDeviceOnly accessibility.
  - Evidence: Apple doc JSON for https://developer.apple.com/documentation/foundation/nsubiquitouskeyvaluestore: 'Don't store personal or sensitive information in the key-value store. The system stores the information on disk in an unencrypted format. Store personal or sensitive information in the person's Keychain instead.' Also 'no more than 1024 keys ... total amount of available storage space for all values is 1 megabyte.' Apple doc JSON for https://developer.apple.com/documentation/security/ksecattrsynchronizable: 'indicates whether the item in question is synchronized to other devices through iCloud' and 'may not also specify a kSecAttrAccessible value that is incompatible with syncing (namely, those whose names end with ThisDeviceOnly).'
- **confirmed**: App Review Guidelines (last updated 16 Oct 2026): 5.1.1(v) apps that support account creation must offer in-app account deletion; 4.8 Google login requires an equivalent privacy-preserving login option; 5.1.2(i) requires disclosure and explicit permission before sharing personal data with third-party AI. Apps with Sign in with Apple should revoke tokens through the REST API on deletion.
  - Evidence: Fetched https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/, footer 'Last Updated: October 16, 2026'. 5.1.1(v): 'If your app supports account creation, you must also offer account deletion within the app.' 4.8 names Google Sign-In among the services that 'must also offer as an equivalent option another login service' that limits data to name and email, allows a private email, and does no ad tracking without consent. 5.1.2(i): 'You must clearly disclose where personal data will be shared with third parties, including with third-party AI, and obtain explicit permission before doing so.' https://developer.apple.com/support/offering-account-deletion-in-your-app/: 'Apps that support Sign in with Apple should use the Sign in with Apple REST API to revoke user tokens.'
- **corrected**: Firestore (us-central1) costs $0.03 per 100K reads, $0.09 per 100K writes and $0.01 per 100K deletes after a free 50K reads, 20K writes and 1 GiB per day/total. Cloud Storage for Firebase is not available on the free Spark plan. Google budgets only alert, and requests keep succeeding over budget.
  - Correct / uncertain: The prices are right for Firestore Standard edition in us-central1. Enterprise edition is priced separately. The free quota is incomplete: per day it is 50,000 reads, 20,000 writes and 20,000 deletes (deletes are also free up to 20K/day), plus 1 GiB stored and 10 GiB outbound per month. It applies only to the one free (default) database per project; named databases get no free quota. Cloud Storage for Firebase requires the Blaze plan: since February 3, 2026, Spark projects cannot use any bucket, including the legacy default one, and calls return 402/403 errors. The budget part is outdated as a blanket statement. Alerts-only budgets do not cap spending. Google Cloud now also offers 'spend cap budgets' that pause a service when its estimated cost passes the budget, but only for the Gemini API, Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (formerly Vertex AI), Cloud Run and Cloud Run functions. Firestore and Cloud Storage are not eligible, so for them requests do keep succeeding over budget unless you build your own Pub/Sub automation that disables billing.
  - Evidence: https://cloud.google.com/firestore/pricing ('Firestore Standard edition pricing'; default location Iowa (us-central1)): 'Document Reads 50,000 $0.03 ... Document Writes 20,000 $0.09 ... Document Deletes 20,000 $0.01 per 100,000 documents'; free tier 'Stored data 1 GiB, Document reads 50,000 per day, Document writes 20,000 per day, Document deletes 20,000 per day, Outbound data transfer 10 GiB per month'; 'Firestore allows exactly one free database per project.' https://firebase.google.com/pricing shows Cloud Storage as 'Not applicable' on Spark. https://firebase.google.com/docs/storage/faqs-storage-changes-announced-sept-2024: 'To use Cloud Storage for Firebase ... you must upgrade to the pay-as-you-go Blaze pricing plan. This requirement went into effect starting February 03, 2026.' https://cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/budgets: 'Setting an alerts-only budget doesn't automatically cap ... usage or spending ... If supported for your service, consider configuring a spend cap budget.' https://cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/budgets-spend-caps lists eligible services: Gemini API, Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (formerly Vertex AI), Cloud Run, Cloud Run functions.
- **confirmed**: Supabase's Apple OAuth (web) flow needs a new Apple secret key every 6 months (the native iOS flow does not), and an auth user who owns Storage objects cannot be deleted until those files are removed.
  - Evidence: https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/social-login/auth-apple: 'If you're using the OAuth flow (web, Flutter web, Kotlin non-iOS platforms), Apple requires you to generate a new secret key every 6 months using the signing key (.p8 file) ... Native-only implementations don't require secret key rotation.' https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/managing-user-data: 'You cannot delete a user if they are the owner of any objects in Supabase Storage ... try deleting all the objects for that user, or reassign ownership to another user.'
- **confirmed**: iCloud in mainland China is operated by GCBD (AIPO Cloud (Guizhou) Technology Co. Ltd.), so CloudKit/iCloud remains available there, unlike Google/Firebase.
  - Evidence: https://support.apple.com/en-us/111754 (published April 15, 2025): 'iCloud in China mainland is operated by GCBD (AIPO Cloud (Guizhou) Technology Co. Ltd). This allows us to continue to improve iCloud services in China mainland and comply with Chinese regulations. iCloud services and all the data you store with iCloud ... will be subject to the terms and conditions of iCloud operated by GCBD.' A search of https://firebase.google.com/support/faq found no statement about availability in China.


## R9. Code porting map (what code is reused on iPad)



## Dream Read to Dream Book (iPad): porting map

Read on 2026-10-20 from `/home/user/meh`, branch `claude/readalong-app` (last commit 05ec382). I read every file in `src/` and changed nothing.

## 0. Short answer

**Code size**

| Folder | Lines | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `src/core` | 9,132 | Pure TypeScript. No Electron, no Node, except two small Node imports. |
| `src/shared` | 869 | Types, defaults and teaching styles. |
| `src/renderer` | 5,286 | React 18 screens, built on the browser page (DOM). |
| `src/web` | 1,635 | The browser version of the bridge, already used by the iPad PWA. |
| `src/main` | 4,044 | Electron main process. Of this, Kokoro is 1,259 lines and speech recognition is 898. |
| `src/preload` | 88 | The Electron bridge. |

**The seam.** The screens talk to the platform through one interface only: `ReadAlongApi` in `src/shared/api.ts`. It has 50 methods. The Mac implements it in `src/preload` plus `src/main`. The PWA implements it in `src/web/api.ts`, which is wrapped in a Proxy so that missing methods do not crash. An iPad app is either:
- a third implementation of the same interface (Capacitor), or
- the same interface turned into native services (React Native or SwiftUI).

**How much code each path can reuse**

| Path | Reuse | What you write new |
|---|---|---|
| (a) Capacitor | About 85–90% | About 6 native plugins. You keep `core`, `shared`, the whole renderer and most of `web`. |
| (b) React Native / Expo | About 55–60% | All screens. You keep `core`, `shared` and the pure helpers. The reader text needs a WebView or a new renderer. |
| (c) Native SwiftUI | About 0% of the code | Everything. The rules, prompts, algorithms and about 650 unit tests become the specification. The one exception is if you embed the TypeScript core with JavaScriptCore. |

**Words used in the tables below**
- **As-is**: copy the file unchanged.
- **Changes**: keep the file, adapt a few platform calls.
- **Replace**: write new iPad code.

---

**Changes Dream Book needs in `shared/styles.ts`**
- Add the learner's own style as the first "character". **`docs/MY-TEACHING-STYLE.md` is not in the code yet.** The `custom` prompt in the code is different: it has no "word ten times", no dictionary-entry step and no RULE THREE.
- Choose the 7 characters.
- RULE ONE maps to `ScriptShape {wordBefore: 3 (the controller already says the word 3 times), wordAfter: 10, sentenceAfterWord: 1}`.
- RULE TWO maps to `{sentenceBefore: 0, sentenceAfter: 2}`.
- RULE THREE ("very easy English") needs a new explain kind, `'easy'`, plus a UI switch. Nothing like it exists today.

## 8. New bridge methods Dream Book needs (not in `api.ts` today)

1. **Account**: `signIn('apple' | 'email')`, `signOut()`, `currentUser()`, `onAuthState(cb)`, and `deleteAccount()`. Deleting the account inside the app is required by App Store guideline 5.1.1(v). If any third-party login is offered, guideline 4.8 also requires a privacy-preserving option such as Sign in with Apple ([guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/)).
2. **Sync**: `syncNow()`, `onSyncState(cb)`, `uploadBookSource(bookId)`, `downloadBookSource(bookId)`. This is what makes "delete the app, reinstall, everything comes back" work. Books sync as the original file (same sha256 id); positions, statuses, vocabulary, settings and characters sync as records.
3. **Whole-book understanding**:
   - `analyzeBook(bookId, {parts, hints, phrases, explanations: 'none' | 'hard' | 'all', easyEnglish})`
   - `bookAnalysis(bookId)`, returning `{parts: [{title, from, to, summary}], characters, hardItems, estUsd}`
   - `onAnalysisProgress(cb)`
   - `cancelAnalysis(bookId)`
4. **Hands-free player** (native):
   - `playerLoad(playlist)`, `playerPlay()`, `playerPause()`, `playerSeek(pos)`
   - `onPlayerProgress(cb)`
   - `setSleepTimer(minutes | 'endOfChapter')`
   - Now Playing metadata, and remote commands (headphones, lock screen)
5. **Level**: `levelObserve(lemma, 'know' | 'dont_know')` and `levelEstimate()`. These wire the existing `LevelModel` into the daily taps.
6. **Review class**: `reviewPlan()`, which wires the existing `core/vocab/review.ts`.
7. **Characters and buttons**: kept in `settings.ai.styles` (already exists). Add `characterOrder` (7 visible) and `buttons` (a customisable button layout).

## 9. Gaps found in the code (useful before porting)

1. `docs/MY-TEACHING-STYLE.md` (commit 05ec382, 2026-10-20) exists only as a document. The `custom` style in `src/shared/styles.ts` is different. RULE THREE has no counterpart.
2. `LevelModel` (`src/core/level/adapt.ts`) is only created when the test ends (`src/renderer/views/LevelTest.tsx`, about line 109). Nothing calls it on "I know" or "I don't know", so the level does not yet adjust day by day, as RULES.md section 7 requires.
3. The review class (`src/core/vocab/review.ts`, `reviewScript.ts`) has no screen or trigger in `src/renderer`.
4. The web hints job has no phrase finder: `hintsPhrases` returns `null` in `src/web/api.ts`, and its cache is v1, against v2 on the Mac.
5. `src/web/tts.ts` has only OpenAI and ElevenLabs, but Settings lists Azure and Google, and `web/index.html` already allows their hosts.
6. Hints run per chapter when the chapter is opened, not for the whole book.
7. The default `anthropicModel` is `claude-opus-5-5`, the most expensive in the code's own price table ($4 in / $20 out per million tokens, as written in `src/main/ai.ts`; not verified today). The whole-book pre-pass should use the hints model (Haiku 5.5, $0.10 / $0.50 per million in that same table).
8. The Kokoro and speech-model downloads come from GitHub release URLs (`src/main/kokoro/download.ts`, `src/main/stt/download.ts`). These need a mirror for users in China.


### Risks in the code for a mobile port


## Risks and gotchas for the iPad port (Dream Book)

**Web search limit.** This run used up its web-search budget before I could search, so I checked facts by fetching first-party pages directly. Verified facts link to their source. Facts marked "(not verified today)" come from my own knowledge or from the repo and should be checked before you rely on them.

## A. Build environment (the biggest blocker for this learner)

**App Store uploads need Xcode 26.**
- Since 28 April 2026, App Store uploads must be built with Xcode 26 or later and the iOS/iPadOS 26 SDK ([Apple upcoming requirements](https://developer.apple.com/news/upcoming-requirements/)).
- Xcode 26.0–26.3 needs macOS Sequoia 15.6 or later. Xcode 26.4.1 to 26.6 needs macOS Tahoe 26.2 or later ([Xcode system requirements](https://developer.apple.com/xcode/system-requirements/)).
- The learner's Intel MacBook Pro on macOS 13 Ventura cannot run any Xcode 26.

**Upgrading the Mac.**
- Whether that Mac can upgrade depends on its exact model. Sequoia supports MacBook Pro 2018 and later. Tahoe 26 is the last macOS for Intel and supports only a few Intel MacBook Pros (not verified today).
- Check: Apple menu → About This Mac.

**Ways around it**
- Build in the cloud: Expo EAS Build (React Native), Xcode Cloud, GitHub Actions macOS runners, Codemagic or Ionic Appflow (Capacitor).
- Or use a newer Apple-silicon Mac.

**What this means for each path**
- **SwiftUI is the hardest path on this Mac.** SwiftUI previews and the Simulator need a local Xcode.
- **Capacitor and React Native** can be developed in a browser or with a dev client, and built in the cloud.

**Accounts and installing**
- The Apple Developer Program costs $99 a year (not verified today).
- Installing on the iPad uses TestFlight, or ad-hoc builds with the device registered.

**Current versions** (from GitHub release pages, fetched today)
- Capacitor stable is 8.5.3 (7 Oct 2026). 8.5.0 (31 Jul 2026) added UIScene support. 9.0.0-alpha.8 is a pre-release ([releases](https://github.com/ionic-team/capacitor/releases)).
- Expo's newest packages are `expo@58.0.16` (19 Oct) ([releases](https://github.com/expo/expo/releases)). I could not confirm which React Native version SDK 58 pairs with.
- React Native stable is 0.88.0 (15 Oct) ([releases](https://github.com/facebook/react-native/releases)).
- ONNX Runtime is 1.31.0 (9 Oct). CoreML can select the Neural Engine on iOS 16+ ([releases](https://github.com/microsoft/onnxruntime/releases)).
- sherpa-onnx is v1.13.8 (10 Sep 2026), with Kokoro voices and a fix for Moonshine v2 hallucinating on silence ([releases](https://github.com/k2-fsa/sherpa-onnx/releases)). It has iOS Swift samples, but React Native only through the third-party `@siteed/sherpa-onnx.rn` ([repo](https://github.com/k2-fsa/sherpa-onnx)).

## B. Background execution: "I just want to sleep and listen"

**The problem.**
- Playback is driven by JavaScript: `Playback.run` loops with `await sleep(250)`, and `ListenController` uses `setTimeout` for the 5-second windows and the 350 ms pauses between repeats.
- **PWA:** `speechSynthesis` stops when the screen locks, and Safari suspends the page. The current PWA cannot do sleep listening.
- **Capacitor:** WKWebView runs in a separate WebContent process, which iOS may throttle or suspend in the background even when the app has the audio background mode. This is a high risk; test it on a real iPad.
- **React Native:** the Hermes JS thread keeps running while the app process is kept alive by an active audio session (verify on a device).
- **SwiftUI:** a native player has no such problem.

**Recommended design (all three paths): "compile, then play".**
- In hands-free mode nobody answers the windows. By RULES.md, silence means "explain", and after the explanation silence means "stays learning, go on". So the whole flow for a chapter is known in advance.
- In the foreground (or on a server), build a playlist for the next chapter: every sentence, plus at each stop the word said 3 times, the explanation, the Chinese meaning, and the sentence re-read. Each item carries its audio file, word timings and sentence key.
- Hand the playlist to a native `AVQueuePlayer`, or an `AVAudioEngine` schedule, with:
  - `UIBackgroundModes: audio`
  - `AVAudioSession` category `.playback`, mode `.spokenAudio`
  - `MPNowPlayingInfoCenter` (title, chapter) and `MPRemoteCommandCenter` (play/pause, previous/next sentence, ±15 s)
  - a sleep timer with fade-out
  - an exact sentence position saved on every item change
- App Store guideline 2.5.4 allows background audio only for real audio playback ([guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/)). **Do not keep the app alive with silent audio while waiting for the AI.** Precompute instead.

**Active mode** (the 5-second microphone windows): keep the live `ListenController`.
- Disable the idle timer so the screen stays on.
- The microphone needs `.playAndRecord` with voice processing, so the tutor's own voice is not recognised.
- The orange microphone indicator will show.
- Recording while the screen is locked is technically possible but fragile and a privacy concern.

**Interruptions** (calls, Siri, AirPods taken out): handle `AVAudioSession` interruption and route-change notifications: pause, keep the position, re-read the sentence from its start (as RULES.md says).

**Network in the background.** It works only while the app is not suspended. A long whole-book AI pass should run on a server, or in the foreground with progress shown. `BGProcessingTask` is opportunistic (often only at night while charging) and not guaranteed.

## C. DOM assumptions in `src/renderer` (they matter for RN and SwiftUI, partly for Capacitor)

**Reader structure**
- `ReaderView` finds words with `querySelector('.s[data-key="c.p.s"] .w[data-t="i"]')`.
- Highlighting is done by adding classes to spans made by `render.ts` (a whole chapter injected through `innerHTML`).
- Selecting text to explain uses `window.getSelection()`.

**Touch conflicts on iPad**
- Double tap means "I know" (`onDoubleClick`). On iPad, a double tap is zoom; `web.css` sets `touch-action: manipulation`.
- A long press opens the iOS text callout (Copy / Look Up / Translate), which fights the custom selection bar.
- Single-tap timing must wait for a possible double tap, which adds about 300 ms.

**Reading mode pagination**
- It uses CSS multi-column (`column-width`, `column-fill: auto`) plus `translateX`.
- The page count comes from `scrollWidth`; the page of a sentence from `getClientRects()`; re-layout from `ResizeObserver`.
- In WebKit, rotation, Split View, Stage Manager and font-size changes all re-layout the whole chapter. Spans that break across two columns can return two rects.
- React Native and SwiftUI have no CSS columns. Keep a WebView for the reading pane, or use TextKit 2 pagination in SwiftUI.

**Other DOM details**
- `zoom: var(--ui-scale)` is used for UI scale (Safari supports `zoom`).
- Hover tooltips (`Tip.tsx`) do not exist on touch.
- Keyboard shortcuts use `KeyboardEvent.code` and need a hardware keyboard. Every action needs an on-screen button, which fits "all buttons customisable".
- `navigator.platform` is "MacIntel" on iPad, so the renderer adds macOS traffic-light space. `src/web/main.ts` already overrides this; keep that.
- Electron-only parts: `webUtils.getPathForFile`, drag and drop of file paths, `-webkit-app-region`, the `menu:action` channel.

## D. Node APIs to remove

| Where | Node API | Replacement |
|---|---|---|
| `src/core/import/pdf.ts` | `import path from 'node:path'` (only `basename`/`extname`) | `src/web/shims/path.ts` |
| `src/main/library.ts` | `zlib` | `DecompressionStream`/`CompressionStream`, or fflate |
| `src/main/library.ts`, `secrets.ts` | `crypto` (createHash, AES-GCM) | `crypto.subtle`, CryptoKit |
| `src/main/kokoro/wav.ts`, `npz.ts` | `Buffer`, JSZip `'nodebuffer'` | `DataView`, `Uint8Array` |
| `src/main/kokoro/engine.ts` | `fs`, `os`, `worker_threads` | Native threads or a Web Worker |
| `src/main/stt/*` | `fs`, `os`, Node streams, `unbzip2-stream`, own tar reader | Not needed with Apple speech recognition |
| `src/main/tts.ts` | `msedge-tts` (Node WebSocket) | Drop the Edge voices |
| `src/main/ai.ts` | `@anthropic-ai/sdk`, `openai` (Node) | `src/web/ai.ts` already replaces them with fetch plus SSE |
| `src/main/index.ts` | `process.env` flags (`READALONG_E2E`, `KOKORO_*`, `STT_*`) | Build-time constants |

**Hermes (React Native) gaps to verify:**
- `Intl.Segmenter` (needed by `segment.ts`; support uncertain)
- `DecompressionStream`
- `TextDecoder('utf-16le')`
- streaming `fetch` bodies (`expo/fetch` should support this; verify)
- pdf.js does not run in Hermes, so use PDFKit.

## E. Performance with large books

**Book size and storage**
- A Book stores every token as an object `{start, end, text, kind}`. A 100,000-word novel is roughly 150,000 tokens: about 10 MB of JSON and roughly 30–60 MB of JS heap (estimate).
- `loadBook` reads the whole book. IndexedDB structured clone of a 10 MB object takes hundreds of milliseconds.
- For native, store sentences in SQLite, compute tokens lazily per chapter, and keep only the open chapter in memory.

**Per-call costs**
- `percentAt` walks the whole book on each call. It is debounced, so this is fine.
- `wordOffsets` and `indexBook` are built once per book.

**Chapter rendering**
- `renderChapter` builds one HTML string per chapter. A 20,000-word chapter means 20,000+ word spans, plus `data-hint` pseudo-elements under hard words.
- With CSS columns this is the slowest moment: opening the chapter, rotating, changing the font.
- Status changes use `restyleLemma` (cheap). Do not re-render the chapter for them.

**PDF import**
- pdf.js keeps every page's text items in memory (`RawPage[]`). A 500-page PDF in WKWebView can hit the WebContent memory limit; the page then goes blank.
- Process page by page, or use PDFKit natively and keep the pure `buildBook`.

**Dictionary and level test**
- The dictionary is 8.4 MB of JSON when unpacked: about 0.3–1 s to parse and tens of MB of heap.
- For native or React Native, convert it to SQLite at build time (`scripts/build-dict.py`).
- `prepareMaterials` for the level test takes about 0.5 s.

**Whole-book AI pass** (needed so that "the AI reads and understands the whole book")
- That means hundreds of requests per book. It must be resumable per chapter (the per-chapter cache already exists), respect 429 rate limits, and show its cost before it starts.
- Hints cost estimates from the code comments (Haiku 5.5 price table in `src/core/ai/hints.ts`; not verified today):
  - about $0.0005 per chapter for hints and about $0.0012 for phrases
  - about $0.10 for a 60-chapter novel
- Pre-generating every explanation for about 1,500 hard items: roughly $0.6 with Haiku 5.5 or roughly $15 with Opus 5.5, at the code's prices (estimate).
- Live explanations with Opus 5.5 cost about $0.01 each (about 2,500 tokens in, 300 out).

## F. Memory on iPad

These figures are estimates; profile on a real device.

| What | Memory or size |
|---|---|
| Kokoro fp16 model | 164 MB on disk; weights cast to fp32 on CPU, about 330 MB plus the ORT arena |
| Moonshine base | about 300 MB RSS (from `docs/VOICE.md`) |
| Parakeet v3 | about 930 MB: too big for the iPad |
| WKWebView with a big chapter and the dictionary | 150–300 MB |

- All together this is about 1 GB or more. That is fine on M-series iPads with 8–16 GB, risky on 3–4 GB iPads (iPad 9th gen has 3 GB, iPad 10th gen 4 GB; not verified today).
- iOS kills the app (jetsam) with no error. Use per-device tiers: on devices under 6 GB, default to the iPad system voices plus Apple speech recognition.
- The entitlement `com.apple.developer.kernel.increased-memory-limit` can help.
- Download model files after install (not in the app bundle). Keep them out of iCloud backup (`isExcludedFromBackup`). Let the learner delete them in Settings.

## G. Voices and speech recognition on iPad

**System voices**
- `AVSpeechSynthesizer` gives word ranges through `speechSynthesizer(_:willSpeakRangeOfSpeechString:utterance:)` ([Apple docs](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/avfaudio/avspeechsynthesizerdelegate/speechsynthesizer(_:willspeakrangeofspeechstring:utterance:)); the page text was not readable, so details are not verified today).
- Ranges are UTF-16 `NSRange`, which matches the JS offsets in `core/model.ts`.
- Enhanced and Premium British voices, and the zh-CN voices for the Chinese meanings, must be downloaded by the learner in iPadOS Settings. Show a guide.

**Kokoro options**
- [kokoro-ios](https://github.com/mlalma/kokoro-ios): MLX Swift, iOS 18+, MIT, per-token timestamps since 1.0.8.
- sherpa-onnx: Kokoro supported, but no per-word timings, so they would be estimated.
- ORT plus a Swift port of `text.ts`, `phonemes.ts` and `align.ts`: the same pipeline as the Mac.

**Licence risk**
- Kokoro's grapheme-to-phoneme step uses espeak-ng, which is GPL-3.0. GPL code inside an App Store app is a known licence conflict.
- Check the licence of the `phonemizer` package and of sherpa-onnx's espeak data before shipping. Alternatives are a dictionary-based G2P or the Apple voices (not verified today).

**Speech recognition**
- Apple SpeechAnalyzer/SpeechTranscriber (iOS 26, on-device) or SFSpeechRecognizer (on-device flag) are free and need no model download. Add `NSSpeechRecognitionUsageDescription` and `NSMicrophoneUsageDescription`. (Not verified today: Apple's pages did not render.)
- Keep `core/voice/commands.ts` for the "I know / I don't know / go on" matching with accent variants. Apple's text output feeds it the same way Moonshine's does.

## H. Account, cloud, China

**Anthropic availability**
- Mainland China, Hong Kong and Macau are not supported regions for Claude.ai or the API ([Anthropic supported countries](https://www.anthropic.com/supported-countries), fetched today).
- The policy also excludes entities headquartered in, or majority-owned from, unsupported regions. Check this for the developer and any company behind Dream Book.
- Do not build a relay that serves users in unsupported regions.
- Keep the AI provider pluggable. The existing `streamOpenAI` with a configurable base URL covers OpenAI-compatible APIs from providers that are available where the learner lives (which providers are legal there: not verified today).
- Apple Intelligence and the Foundation Models framework are, as far as I know, not available in mainland China (not verified today).

**China App Store storefront**
- Generative-AI apps on the China storefront need government filings: an ICP filing number and an AI-service filing (not verified today; Apple's guidelines page did not show it).
- The simplest option is to leave the China storefront out at first.

**Cloud choice**
- **CloudKit plus Sign in with Apple** is the most "everything comes back after reinstall" option. It needs no server, records live in the user's iCloud, and iCloud works in mainland China, where it is run by a local partner (not verified today).
- Firebase and Google Cloud are blocked in mainland China.
- I could not reach supabase.com today to check its free-tier limits.
- CloudKit from Capacitor: use CloudKit JS or a small native plugin. From React Native: a native module. From SwiftUI: SwiftData with CloudKit, or `CKSyncEngine`.
- Sync records with the same JSON shapes the Mac writes (`docs/IPAD.md` section 5 already designed this: same sha256 book ids, same `Position`). Merge rules exist in `mergeEntry`; for the rest, the newest record wins.

**Keys**
- Use the Keychain. Items marked synchronizable return through iCloud Keychain.
- For "very easy" use, a Dream Book server with the developer's own key plus a subscription (in-app purchase) removes key setup for the learner. Apple takes 15–30% (not verified today).

**App Store rules**
- Account deletion must be possible inside the app: guideline 5.1.1(v).
- If a third-party login is offered, guideline 4.8 requires a privacy-preserving login option such as Sign in with Apple ([guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/)).

## I. Smaller gotchas

- **Content Security Policy.** The renderer's `index.html` CSP allows `connect-src 'self' app: blob: data:` only. The web build's `web/index.html` already adds the AI and voice hosts and `'wasm-unsafe-eval'`. Capacitor must use the web one, plus the sync and auth hosts.
- **Storage limits.** IndexedDB inside WKWebView can be cleared by the system under storage pressure (not verified today). Do not keep the only copy of a learner's vocabulary there; sync it.
- **Service worker.** Remove `sw.js` and the install hint in Capacitor; they are not needed and can serve stale files.
- **Microphone in WKWebView.** `getUserMedia` plus an AudioWorklet from a Blob URL works in WKWebView, but echo cancellation is weaker than native voice processing, and permission prompts can repeat. Let the native STT plugin own the microphone.
- **Ids.** Keep the sha256 book-id scheme (first 24 hex characters) and `sentenceKey` "c.p.s" on every platform. Every cache, position and vocabulary entry depends on them.
- **Tests.** Port or keep `test/unit` (about 650 tests): `controller`, `playback`, `script-rules`, `segment`, `pdf`, `epub`, `hints-phrases` and others. For SwiftUI they are the specification; for Capacitor and React Native they keep running in vitest unchanged.

# Appendix B: Full research on voices and similar apps

The raw research and fact-checks behind Part 3 and Part 4.

### Raw research: apps

#### Summary
I looked at 16 apps that are like Dream Book. I ran 54 web searches; the search limit stopped me after that. Direct page fetches did not work, so most facts come from search results with links. Five main findings:

(1) Where the build method is known, the top apps are native. Speechify uses Swift (from its iOS job posts). Duolingo uses Swift. Blinkist moved from Objective-C to Swift. Kindle is partly React Native. For ElevenReader, Readwise, Calm, LingQ and Audible I found no evidence either way.

(2) No app reads a book aloud and also explains hard words by itself, in context, while you listen. Speechify and Kindle "Ask this Book" only answer when you ask. LingQ and Readlang only explain when you tap. This is Dream Book's unique feature.

(3) The listening apps share the same basic features:
- word-by-word highlighting in time with the voice
- a sleep timer
- playback that continues when the screen is locked
- offline listening for paying users only
- audio that is made once and then replayed for free (ElevenReader works this way)

(4) Prices are close to each other:
- language readers: $48 to $120 a year
- listening apps: $99 to $139 a year
- sleep apps: $60 to $70 a year

The biggest complaints are about billing (surprise yearly charges, Voice Dream's 2024 switch to a subscription), robotic free voices and free plans with small limits.

(5) A sleep-mode learner needs four things above all:
- playback that never stops all night
- a calm voice that works offline
- the app noticing when you fall asleep, so it does not explain words to nobody
- a short review in the morning

The suggested prices are: Free (offline voices, 10 AI explanations a day), Plus $6.99 a month or $49.99 a year, Premium $14.99 a month or $119.99 a year. The AI costs about $0.015 per listening hour with Claude Haiku 5.5. It costs about $0.25 per hour with Sonnet 5.5.

## 2. The most useful lessons from each app
- **ElevenReader: the best business model to copy.** Users pay for *making* audio, not for *listening*. Audio is made once and replays are free, so nightly re-listening costs nothing. The sleep timer is free; offline listening is paid.
- **Speechify: the closest competitor.** Since January 2026 its **Voice AI Assistant on iOS** lets you talk with a document, get quizzes and summaries, and make podcasts ([9to5Mac](https://9to5mac.com/2026/01/12/speechify-launches-voice-ai-assistant-on-ios/)). But it only answers when you ask; it never stops the story to teach a hard word. Copy its skip panel and its speed control. Do **not** copy its billing.
- **Kindle "Ask this Book": the spoiler-free rule.** Answers only use the text up to your current position. Dream Book currently sends about 200 words *after* the position. Keep those words for meaning, but tell the AI never to reveal what happens later. **Recaps / "Story so far"** is the right idea for a morning "where was I" feature.
- **Whispersync: reading and listening share one position.** Dream Read already does this between its two modes. The next step is the same between Mac and iPad (sync).
- **Voice Dream:**
  - Copy the **pronunciation dictionary** (fix how character names are said).
  - Copy **"keeps reading with the screen locked"**.
  - Copy **word plus line highlighting**.
  - Lesson: if you ever change a paid app to a subscription, **let old buyers keep what they paid for**.
- **LingQ and Readlang: the learning layer.**
  - LingQ: word statuses (Dream Read already has them), known-word milestones, spaced repetition.
  - Readlang: cheap, clear tiers, with the free plan at **10 explanations a day**.
- **Duolingo: habits.** Use a streak with **freezes and revival**. Streaks work through "loss aversion" (losing feels worse than winning feels good), but guides warn not to make losing a streak painful ([appstorys](https://appstorys.com/blog-Streaks-Milestones-Habit-Gamification)). Guilt notifications ("Your streak is in danger!") are criticised as manipulation ([WebdesignerDepot](https://webdesignerdepot.com/the-art-of-duolingo-notifications-the-subtle-manipulation-of-language-learners/)). One study found the system builds dependence on the app, not habits that last on their own ([case study](https://www.wr-publishing.org/index.php/ijmat/article/view/908)).
- **Calm and other sleep stories: how sleep audio sounds.**
  - Slow pacing (test at **120–140 words per minute**).
  - No cliffhangers and no sudden sounds.
  - Sessions of 20–45 minutes.
  - These rules come from a community skill, which is a weak source ([sleep-story skill](https://claudeskills.info/skills/jwynia/agent-skills/sleep-story/)).
  - For Dream Book: in sleep mode, use a slower speed, longer pauses between sentences, quieter explanations, and a fade-out at the end.
- **iOS 26 "Pause Media When Falling Asleep":** AirPods 4 and AirPods Pro 2/3 can sense that you fell asleep and pause the audio. Sources disagree on whether it is on by default ([Macworld](https://www.macworld.com/article/2835295/ios-26-feature-that-turns-off-headphones-when-you-fall-asleep-isnt-limited-to-airpods.html), [iGeeksBlog](https://www.igeeksblog.com/airpods-auto-pause-when-you-fall-asleep/)). Dream Book should treat that pause as a "fell asleep here" signal.

---
## 3. How they are built, and what that means for Dream Book
- **What I found:** Speechify, Duolingo, Blinkist, Voice Dream and BookPlayer are native Swift. Kindle is partly React Native. I found no evidence for ElevenReader, Readwise, Calm, LingQ or Audible. I found **no Flutter evidence** for any of them.
- **Why Dream Book should be native, not a PWA:** the sleep-mode features need things only a native app can do.
  - **Playback all night with the screen off:** `AVAudioSession` playback, Now Playing on the lock screen, remote commands.
  - **Listening to the microphone with the screen locked**, for voice commands: the "audio" background mode plus the microphone usage text. iOS shows a recording indicator ([Vivox iOS docs](https://docs.unity.com/en-us/vivox-core/developer-guide/ios/ios-requirements)).
    - One developer found speech stopped on lock even with background audio turned on, and had to work around it ([Apple forum](https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/849627)). So **test on a real iPad with the screen locked** early.
  - **The free Kokoro voice on the iPad itself:**
    - A Swift CoreML package (about 80 MB INT8, about 170 MB first download) ([soniqo](https://soniqo.audio/guides/kokoro)).
    - A CoreML conversion measured on iOS 26.5 in June 2026 (self-reported) ([HF](https://huggingface.co/mattmireles/kokoro-coreml)).
    - An MLX Swift port, about **3.3x faster than real time on iPhone 13 Pro**, needs iOS 18 ([kokoro-ios](https://swiftpackageregistry.com/mlalma/kokoro-ios)).
    - **Caution:** KOKORO.md says only the kokoro-onnx export gives the `duration` output that Dream Read uses for word timing. Check whether the CoreML or MLX ports give durations. If not, run the same ONNX model with ONNX Runtime for iOS (not tested).
- **Three ways to build it, fastest first:**
  - **(A) Capacitor shell:** wrap the existing web app (`src/renderer` plus `src/web`) and add native Swift plugins for audio and sleep, the microphone and speech recognition, and Kokoro. This keeps almost all current UI and logic.
  - **(B) Native SwiftUI screens** that run the existing TypeScript `src/core` inside JavaScriptCore. This keeps the about 650 tested core functions.
  - **(C) Full Swift rewrite.** Best quality, most work.
  - For a non-developer working with AI assistants, **(A) then (B)** is the realistic path. This advice comes from general knowledge, not from my searches.
- **Your Intel Mac on macOS 13 may be a blocker. UNVERIFIED:** the search limit stopped me before I could check. From memory: the App Store now requires apps built with recent Xcode and SDK versions, and Xcode 26 needs macOS 15.6 or newer. Check this first. If it is true, you would need to update macOS (if your MacBook model allows it) or use a cloud build service (Xcode Cloud, GitHub Actions macOS runners, Expo EAS, Codemagic).

## 5. iPad design to copy
- **Listening layout:** lyrics-style lines, big current sentence, word highlight (ElevenReader, LingQ, Beelinguapp karaoke).
  - Landscape: text on the left, word card and tutor transcript on the right (a side column).
  - Portrait: the card slides up from the bottom.
  - Support Split View and Stage Manager, and the existing keyboard shortcuts.
- **Night theme:** true black, a dimmer that goes very low, no bright flashes when the card appears.
- **Sleep timer behind a moon button** (Audible, Apple Books, ElevenReader, Voice Dream):
  - presets 15, 30, 45 and 60 minutes
  - **End of chapter** (Audible)
  - **after this explanation** (new)
  - a 30–60 second **fade-out**
  - an "extend 15 min" button
- **Lock screen:** Now Playing with the book, chapter and cover. While paused at a word, put the word and its Chinese meaning in the subtitle line. A Live Activity on iPad is possible (iPadOS support: UNVERIFIED, from memory).
- **Widgets:** "Continue last night" and "Words from last night".
- **CarPlay:** not relevant on iPad. Add it later for iPhone (Audible has it).
